newsitem.title: USA: US delays action against EU meat imports two weeks.
newsitem.headline: US delays action against EU meat imports two weeks.

text.p: The United States has extended its deadline for action against meat imports from the European Union by two weeks, an Agriculture Department official said Tuesday.

The USDA official confirmed earlier reports from Brussels that Washington has decided to delay removing some 100 European meat and poultry packing plants from its list of approved exporters in hopes that an agreement could be reached in continuing talks between the EU and U.S. over meat inspection regulations.
The threatened action by Washington could halt the flow of up to $300 million worth of EU meat shipments to the United States, mostly pork products from Denmark and Italian ham.

EU negotiators are returning to Washington Wednesday to continue the so-called veterinary equivalency talks. Negotiators ended face-to-face talks last Friday and kept in contact over the weekend through faxes and phone calls.
Failure to reach an agreement in the meat talks has resulted in a nasty trade dispute that threatens hundreds of millions of dollars worth of bilateral trade.

Since April 1, U.S. poultry exports to Europe have been blocked because of new inspection regulations recently imposed by the EU. Some $50 million worth of U.S. poultry is exported every year to the EU.

Poultry issues have remained the key sticking point in the negotiations. While progress has reportedly been made in several other non-poultry areas, U.S. and EU officials still appear to be in disagreement over how the U.S. poultry industry decontaminates carcasses with a chlroine solution

Many U.S. meat industry sources had anticipated Monday that USDA would avert a full-blown trade war with the European Union by agreeing to accept a deal in the meat talks on everything accept the poultry issues.
The U.S. poultry industry said this would be an unacceptable move, and it would not support such a decision.
The EU recently proposed to undertake a scientific study with the U.S. of decontaminants in the slaughter and packing process, but did not include chlorine in the the proposed study.
